newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danes say British TV presenter was bomb target.
newsitem.headline: Danes say British TV presenter was bomb target.

text.p: Danish police said on Monday that letter bombs posted by suspected neo-Nazis were addressed to a British television presenter whose husband is black and to a British anti-fascist group.

They said one was also addressed to the British neo-Nazi group Combat 18, to which the Danish suspects themselves are believed to be linked, in what may have been an attempt to disguise the identity of the sender.

Danish detectives arrested a group of seven suspected local neo-Nazis at the weekend after police seized three letter bombs -- explosive devices hidden in video cassettes -- posted in Sweden to addresses in London.
They said letters were addressed to former Olympic swimming star Sharron Davies and to Anti-Fascist Action, an umbrella organisation of European groups fighting right-wing militants.
British newspapers said that former heavyweight boxing champion Frank Bruno and England international footballer Paul Ince were also targetted.
Bruno and Ince are black while their wives, Laura and Claire, are white. Davies is white and is married to black athlete Derek Redmond.
Combat 18 has a violent history and is named after the first and eighth letters of the alphabet, A and H -- the initials of Adolf Hitler.
On the alleged addressing of a letter bomb to Combat 18, Danish police were pursuing several theories.

"One theory is that there is an internal power struggle within the Combat 18 organisation -- we know that there has been internal fighting in Nazi circles," Copenhagen murder squad chief Kurt Jensen told the Danish news agency Ritzau.

"Another possiblity is that they were trying to disguise the identity of the sender. Combat 18 in London could have been warned in advance and it would have appeared as someone else was behind the letter bombs," Jensen said.

The latest Danish police statement followed conflicting statements in which Danish Justice Minister Frank Jensen said that the bombs were aimed at British leftists and sports personalities in mixed-race marriages but police later said there was no evidence that a British athlete was involved.
